title: Clement Greenberg and Formalism
welcome_lead: Medium-specificity and the flatness of the picture plane.
meta_desc: A-Level Art & Design: Clement Greenberg, formalism, and modernist criticism.

concepts.def: American critic (1909-1994), champion of Abstract Expressionism.
Criticism focused on visual form — line, colour, composition, surface.
Greenberg's idea that each art form should explore its own essential nature.
1960 Greenberg essay arguing painting must assert its flatness.
Greenberg's 1939 term for popular, sentimental, mass-produced culture.

walkthroughs.body_html: In 1939, Clement Greenberg distinguished avant-garde art (formally rigorous, self-critical) from kitsch (mass culture, ersatz emotion). The essay set his lifelong critical position.
Greenberg argued each medium must explore its essential characteristics. For painting, this meant flatness — abandoning illusion of depth. Pollock's drips and Rothko's colour fields exemplified this.
Postmodernists Rosalind Krauss and T.J. Clark dismantled Greenbergian purity, arguing meaning is social, not formal. Yet his attention to surface and material remains fundamental to A-Level analysis.
